cards.title: The big three
cards.body: Every food you eat is mostly some mix of three macronutrients: protein, carbohydrates, and fat. They each do different jobs, and your body needs all three. No single macro is the villain — balance is the whole game.

cards.title: Protein: the builder
cards.body: Protein repairs muscle, skin, hair, and nails, and it keeps you full longer than carbs. Aim for a palm-sized portion at each meal: chicken, fish, eggs, beans, lentils, tofu, Greek yogurt. Most adults do well around 1.2 to 2 grams per kilo of body weight daily.

cards.title: Carbs: the fuel
cards.body: Carbohydrates are your body's preferred energy source, especially for your brain. Whole versions — oats, rice, potatoes, fruit — come with fiber that slows digestion and steadies energy. Refined ones — soda, candy — spike and crash you.

cards.title: Fat: not the enemy
cards.body: Fat helps you absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K, protects organs, and makes food satisfying. Favor unsaturated sources: olive oil, nuts, avocado, fatty fish. Trans fats (partially hydrogenated oils) are the ones worth avoiding.
The hand method, no scale needed: a palm of protein, a fist of vegetables, a cupped hand of carbs, a thumb of fats. It's rough, it's portable, and it beats guessing.

cards.q: Which macro is mainly responsible for building and repairing muscle?
cards.explain: Protein supplies the amino acids your body uses to build and repair tissue. Carbs fuel you and fats support hormones and vitamins, but building is protein's job.

flashcards.front: Which macro keeps you fullest the longest?
flashcards.back: Protein — it digests slowly and steadies hunger.

flashcards.front: Name a whole-carb and a refined-carb example.
flashcards.back: Whole: oats or brown rice. Refined: soda or candy.
Unsaturated: olive oil, nuts, avocado, fatty fish. Avoid trans fats.

questions.q: Why does protein keep you full longer than carbs?
questions.explain: Protein's slow digestion and hormonal effects on satiety outlast quick-burning carbs.
The brain runs primarily on glucose from carbs. It can adapt to alternatives, but carbs are its first choice.

questions.q: Which fat source is the best pick?
questions.explain: Olive oil is rich in unsaturated fats. Partially hydrogenated oils contain trans fats linked to heart disease.

questions.q: Using the hand method, a serving of vegetables is...
questions.explain: Fist of veg, palm of protein, cupped hand of carbs, thumb of fats — the whole system fits in your hands.

questions.q: Refined carbs differ from whole carbs mainly in...
choices: Fiber content and how fast they digest
questions.explain: Refining strips fiber, so the carbs hit your bloodstream fast — spike, crash, hunger again.

cards.title: The serving-size trap
cards.body: The first thing on any label is the serving size — and it's often smaller than what you'd actually eat. A '200-calorie' snack pack with 2.5 servings is really 500 calories. Always multiply before you judge.

cards.title: Sugar's many aliases
cards.body: Ingredients list anything ending in -ose (fructose, dextrose), plus syrup, nectar, cane juice, and maltodextrin — all sugar wearing costumes. If three of the first five ingredients are sweeteners by different names, it's dessert.

cards.title: % Daily Value, decoded
cards.body: The %DV column tells you how much of a nutrient one serving provides against a 2,000-calorie day. Rule of thumb: 5% or less is low, 20% or more is high. Useful for spotting sodium and fiber at a glance.
Ingredients are listed by weight, heaviest first. If sugar (by any name) is in the top three, the product is mostly sugar — no matter what the front of the box promises.

Compare two yogurts: Cup A lists 'strawberry, milk, sugar' with 12g sugar per 100g. Cup B lists 'milk, sugar, glucose syrup, strawberry flavor' with 18g sugar. Same front-of-box claims, very different insides. The label never lies; marketing does.

cards.q: What's the first thing you should check on a nutrition label?
cards.explain: Every other number on the label is per serving. If the serving is unrealistically small, all the numbers mislead you until you multiply.

flashcards.front: Why does serving size matter most?
flashcards.back: All label numbers are per serving — multiply by what you'll actually eat.

flashcards.front: Name three hidden names for sugar.
flashcards.back: Any three of: fructose, dextrose, syrup, nectar, cane juice, maltodextrin, anything ending in -ose.
One serving gives 20% of that nutrient for a 2,000-calorie day — that's high.

flashcards.front: How are ingredients ordered on a label?

questions.q: A bag says 150 calories, 3 servings per bag. You eat the whole bag. Calories?
questions.explain: 150 × 3 servings = 450. The front number is per serving, not per package.

questions.q: 'Evaporated cane juice' on an ingredient list is...
questions.explain: It's sugar with a health-food costume. The -ose family and syrups are all added sugars.

questions.q: A soup has 25% DV sodium per serving. That means...
questions.explain: 20%+ DV is the 'high' threshold. One serving already covers a quarter of the day's sodium.

questions.q: Sugar is the second ingredient listed. That tells you...
choices: It's one of the heaviest ingredients by weight
questions.explain: Ingredients descend by weight, so #2 means there's a lot of it in there.

questions.q: Best quick check for fiber on a label?
questions.explain: %DV gives you the fact; front-of-box claims give you the marketing.

cards.title: The plate method
cards.body: Forget counting: fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with protein, and a quarter with carbs. Add a thumb of healthy fats. It auto-balances macros without an app, a scale, or a spreadsheet.

cards.title: Prep beats willpower
cards.body: Decide once, eat well all week: cook a big batch of grains, roast a tray of vegetables, and prep two proteins on Sunday. Weeknight you becomes an assembler, not a chef. Hungry brains make bad food decisions; prepped food removes the decision.

Shop the perimeter of the grocery store: produce, meat, dairy, bakery. The middle aisles are where the ultra-processed stuff lives. You don't have to avoid them entirely — just start outside and work in.

A sample day on the plate method: breakfast — Greek yogurt, berries, oats, handful of nuts. Lunch — big salad, grilled chicken, olive oil, a roll. Dinner — salmon, roasted broccoli, sweet potato. Snacks — apple, handful of almonds. Nothing counted, everything balanced.

cards.title: The 80/20 reality
cards.body: Eat well 80% of the time and the other 20% genuinely doesn't matter. The all-or-nothing mindset is what kills diets — one pizza doesn't ruin anything, but 'I already failed' thinking ruins everything.

cards.q: On the plate method, how much of the plate is vegetables?
cards.explain: Half the plate is vegetables. That single rule crowds out the less nutritious stuff without any counting.

flashcards.back: Half veg, quarter protein, quarter carbs, plus a thumb of healthy fats.
It removes decisions when you're hungry — you assemble instead of improvising.

flashcards.front: Where should you start grocery shopping?
flashcards.back: The perimeter: produce, meat, dairy, bakery.

flashcards.front: What is the 80/20 rule of eating?
flashcards.back: Eat well 80% of the time; the other 20% doesn't matter. Consistency beats perfection.

questions.q: Why does the plate method work without counting calories?
choices: Vegetables crowd out calorie-dense food automatically
questions.explain: Half a plate of veg physically limits room for denser foods while adding fiber and volume.

questions.q: Biggest benefit of Sunday meal prep?
questions.explain: Decision fatigue is the enemy. Prepped components turn weeknight cooking into assembly.

questions.q: Someone eats perfectly all week then has pizza Friday. Verdict?
questions.explain: 80/20 means one indulgent meal is part of the plan, not a failure. The all-or-nothing spiral is the real diet killer.

questions.q: Best first step for a beginner meal planner?
choices: Cook grains + roast veg + prep two proteins weekly
questions.explain: Three batch-cooked components cover most meals. Supplements and purges are distractions.

choices: Whole foods live there; ultra-processed fills the middle aisles
questions.explain: Produce, meat, dairy, and bakery ring the store. The center aisles are engineered snack territory.
